stem: What is meant by a **pure-breeding** organism?

options.content: One that is heterozygous for a gene, so it passes both alleles to its offspring
options.rationale: Heterozygous organisms pass on two different alleles, so they do not breed true.

options.content: One that is homozygous for a gene, so it passes the same allele to all its offspring
options.rationale: Pure-breeding means homozygous.

options.content: One that shows the dominant phenotype
options.rationale: A dominant phenotype can come from a heterozygous genotype, which is not pure-breeding.

options.content: One that was produced by asexual reproduction, so it is identical to its parent
options.rationale: Pure-breeding describes the genotype of a gene, not the way the organism was produced.

explanation: A pure-breeding organism is homozygous (for example RR or rr), so all its gametes carry the same allele. Crossed with a similar organism, it always produces offspring like itself.
hints: 'Pure' means the alleles are the same.

stem: In a breeding experiment, what is the **F1 generation**?

options.content: The offspring of a cross between the two parents
options.rationale: F1 is the first generation of offspring.

options.content: The two parents used at the start of the experiment
options.rationale: The parents are the P generation.

options.content: The offspring of crossing two F2 individuals
options.rationale: Crossing F1 individuals gives the F2; crossing F2 individuals gives the F3.

options.content: The dominant allele of the gene
options.rationale: F1 names a generation, not an allele.

explanation: The parents are the P generation, their offspring the F1, and the offspring of crossing F1 individuals together the F2.
hints: F stands for 'filial', meaning offspring.

stem: In cattle, polled (**P**) is dominant to horned (**p**). True or false: when two heterozygous polled cattle (**Pp**) are mated, about one quarter of their calves are expected to be horned.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Correct. Pp × Pp gives 1 PP : 2 Pp : 1 pp, so 1 in 4 calves is expected to be horned (pp).
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: It is true. Each parent passes on p in half of its gametes, so 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4 of the calves are expected to be pp (horned).

explanation: Each Pp parent makes P and p gametes in equal numbers. The Punnett square gives PP, Pp, Pp and pp: 3 polled : 1 horned, so one quarter of the calves are expected to be horned.
hints: Draw a Punnett square for Pp × Pp.

stem: In pea plants, tall (**T**) is dominant to dwarf (**t**). A plant with genotype **Tt** is crossed with a plant with genotype **tt**. What is the expected ratio of tall to dwarf offspring?

options.rationale: 3 : 1 comes from crossing two heterozygous plants (Tt × Tt).
All tall would need one parent to be TT.
Tt gives T or t; tt gives only t: offspring Tt and tt in equal numbers.
Only two genotypes are possible, Tt and tt, in equal numbers.

explanation: The Tt parent makes T and t gametes in equal numbers; the tt parent makes only t. Offspring: Tt (tall) and tt (dwarf) in a 1 : 1 ratio.
hints: List the gametes of each parent first.

stem: In pea plants, the allele for purple flowers is dominant to the allele for white flowers. Two plants that are both **heterozygous** for flower colour are crossed. What percentage of the offspring are expected to have **white** flowers?
explanation: Using W (purple) and w (white): Ww × Ww gives WW, Ww, Ww and ww. Only ww is white: 1 in 4, which is 25%.
workedSolution:
1. Each heterozygous parent (Ww) makes W and w gametes in equal numbers.
2. Offspring: 1 WW : 2 Ww : 1 ww.
3. White flowers (ww) $= \frac{1}{4} \times 100 = 25\%$.
hints: White is the recessive phenotype.

stem: In peas, yellow seeds (**Y**) are dominant to green seeds (**y**). Which cross could produce some plants with **green** seeds?

options.rationale: Every offspring receives Y from the YY parent, so all are Yy (yellow).
Every offspring receives Y from the YY parent, so none can be yy.
All offspring are YY, with yellow seeds.
Each parent can pass on y, so 1 in 4 offspring are expected to be yy (green).

explanation: A green-seeded plant must be yy, so it needs a y allele from each parent. Only the Yy × Yy cross allows both parents to pass on y.
hints: What genotype must a green-seeded plant have?

stem: In pea plants, tall (**T**) is dominant to dwarf (**t**). Complete the description of a cross between a heterozygous tall plant and a dwarf plant. Type each allele exactly, using capital or small letters.

payload.template: The tall plant (Tt) makes gametes that carry T or {{blank:g1}}. All the gametes of the dwarf plant carry {{blank:g2}}. The offspring have the genotypes Tt and {{blank:o}}, in a 1 : 1 ratio, so {{blank:pc}} % of the offspring are expected to be dwarf.

explanation: Tt makes T and t gametes; tt makes only t gametes. The offspring are Tt (tall) and tt (dwarf) in equal numbers, so 50% are expected to be dwarf.
hints: A dwarf plant must be homozygous recessive.

stem: In cattle, polled (**P**) is dominant to horned (**p**). Match each cross with the expected phenotypes of the calves.
explanation: PP × pp gives all Pp (polled). Pp × Pp gives 3 polled : 1 horned. Pp × pp gives 1 polled : 1 horned. pp × pp gives all pp (horned). No monohybrid cross with complete dominance gives 1 polled : 3 horned.
hints: Work out the gametes of each parent, then the offspring.

stem: A pure-breeding tall pea plant is crossed with a pure-breeding dwarf pea plant. The F1 plants are then crossed with each other. Which row shows the expected phenotypes of the F1 and the F2?

options.content: F1: all tall. F2: 1 tall : 1 dwarf
options.rationale: A 1 : 1 ratio would need one of the parents of the F2 to be tt, but both F1 parents are Tt.

options.content: F1: all tall. F2: 3 tall : 1 dwarf
options.rationale: TT × tt gives all Tt; Tt × Tt gives 3 tall : 1 dwarf.

options.content: F1: 1 tall : 1 dwarf. F2: 3 tall : 1 dwarf
options.rationale: Pure-breeding parents (TT and tt) can only give Tt offspring, all tall.

options.content: F1: all of medium height. F2: 1 tall : 2 medium : 1 dwarf
options.rationale: With complete dominance the heterozygote is tall, not intermediate.

explanation: TT × tt gives F1 plants that are all Tt and tall. Crossing two F1 plants (Tt × Tt) gives 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt, which is 3 tall : 1 dwarf in the F2.
hints: Pure-breeding means homozygous: TT and tt.

stem: In cattle, polled (**P**) is dominant to horned (**p**). Over several years a farmer near Gweru mates heterozygous polled bulls with heterozygous polled cows and gets 48 calves. How many of the calves would you expect to be **horned**?
explanation: Pp × Pp gives 3 polled : 1 horned, so one quarter of the calves are expected to be horned: $\frac{1}{4} \times 48 = 12$.
workedSolution:
1. Pp × Pp gives offspring 1 PP : 2 Pp : 1 pp.
2. Horned (pp) is 1 out of every 4 offspring.
3. Expected horned calves $= \frac{1}{4} \times 48 = 12$.
hints: What fraction of the offspring of Pp × Pp are pp?

stem: The allele for normal skin pigment (**A**) is dominant to the allele for albinism (**a**). A couple are both heterozygous (**Aa**). What is the probability that their first child will have albinism? Give your answer as a fraction, a decimal or a percentage.

rejected.feedback: Each parent passes on a with a probability of 1/2, so the chance of aa is 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.
That is a ratio. The probability is 1/4 (0.25 or 25%).
3/4 is the probability that the child does not have albinism.

explanation: Aa × Aa gives AA, Aa, Aa and aa. Only aa has albinism, so the probability is $\frac{1}{4}$ (0.25 or 25%).
hints: Draw a Punnett square for Aa × Aa.

stem: A heterozygous tall pea plant (**Tt**) is self-pollinated, and 160 plants are grown from its seeds. How many of these plants would you expect to be **heterozygous**?
explanation: Tt × Tt gives 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt, so half of the offspring are expected to be heterozygous: $\frac{2}{4} \times 160 = 80$.
workedSolution:
1. Self-pollination crosses the plant with itself: Tt × Tt.
2. Offspring genotypes: 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt.
3. Heterozygous (Tt) $= \frac{2}{4} \times 160 = 80$ plants.
hints: Heterozygous means Tt, not 'tall'.

stem: In a family, two parents who do not have albinism have a child with albinism. What does this show?

options.content: The allele for albinism is recessive, and both parents are heterozygous.
options.rationale: The allele was hidden in both parents, and each passed it on.

options.content: The allele for albinism is dominant, and both parents are homozygous.
options.rationale: A dominant allele would show in any parent who carried it.

options.content: Only one parent carries the allele for albinism.
options.rationale: A recessive feature needs the allele from both parents.

options.content: The child's albinism was caused by the environment, not by genes.
options.rationale: Albinism is inherited; it is not caused by the environment.

explanation: The child is homozygous recessive (aa) and received a from each parent. As neither parent has albinism, each must be Aa, with the recessive allele hidden by the dominant one.
hints: How can an allele be present in a parent but not show?

stem:
The table describes a family tree (pedigree) for albinism. The allele for normal pigment (**A**) is dominant to the allele for albinism (**a**).

| Generation | Person | Sex | Has albinism? | Parents |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| I | Farai | male | no | — |
| I | Chipo | female | no | — |
| II | Tatenda | male | yes | Farai and Chipo |
| II | Rudo | female | no | Farai and Chipo |
| II | Nyasha | female | no | Farai and Chipo |
| II | Kudakwashe | male | yes | (from another family; married to Rudo) |
| III | Tinashe | male | yes | Rudo and Kudakwashe |
| III | Ruvimbo | female | no | Rudo and Kudakwashe |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Explain how the information about Farai, Chipo and Tatenda shows that the allele for albinism is recessive.

points.description: Farai and Chipo do not have albinism but their son Tatenda does
So the allele must have been present but hidden (masked) in both parents; a hidden allele is recessive / both parents are carriers (heterozygous)

parts.explanation: Farai and Chipo do not have albinism, but their son Tatenda does. Tatenda must have inherited the allele for albinism from both parents, so both parents carry it without showing it. An allele that is present but hidden by another allele is recessive.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Give the genotypes of Farai and Chipo.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Give Rudo's genotype. Type the letters exactly, using a capital and a small letter where needed.

rejected.feedback: Rudo has a child with albinism (Tinashe), so she must carry a: her genotype is Aa.
Rudo does not have albinism, so she has at least one A allele.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: What is the probability that Rudo and Kudakwashe's next child will have albinism? Give a fraction, a decimal or a percentage.

rejected.feedback: Kudakwashe is aa, so every child gets a from him; the chance depends only on Rudo (Aa): 1/2.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Nyasha does not have albinism. What is the probability that she is heterozygous (**Aa**)?

options.rationale: 1/4 is the chance of a child of Aa × Aa being aa.
1/2 is the chance for any child of Aa × Aa, but we already know Nyasha is not aa.
Of the three combinations without albinism (AA, Aa, Aa), two are Aa.
3/4 is the chance of a child not having albinism, not of being a carrier.

explanation: Tatenda (aa) has unaffected parents, so the allele is recessive and Farai and Chipo are both Aa. Rudo has a child with albinism, so she is Aa; with Kudakwashe (aa) each child has a 1/2 chance of being aa. Nyasha is AA or Aa; two of the three equally likely unaffected combinations are Aa, so her chance of being a carrier is 2/3.
workedSolution:
1. (a) Unaffected parents (Farai, Chipo) with an affected child (Tatenda): the allele was hidden in both parents, so it is recessive.
2. (b) Tatenda is aa, with one a from each parent; neither parent has albinism, so both are Aa.
3. (c) Rudo has no albinism (at least one A) but her son Tinashe is aa, so she passed on a: Rudo is Aa.
4. (d) Aa × aa gives Aa, Aa, aa, aa: probability of aa $= \frac{2}{4} = \frac{1}{2}$.
5. (e) Aa × Aa gives AA, Aa, aA, aa. Nyasha is not aa, so she is one of AA, Aa, aA: probability of being heterozygous $= \frac{2}{3}$.
hints: Start with a person with albinism: you know their genotype for certain.
For (e), remove the combination that Nyasha cannot have.

stem: A student wants to find out whether a tall pea plant is **TT** or **Tt**. Which plant should she cross it with?

options.content: Another tall plant of unknown genotype
options.rationale: Two unknowns cannot reveal the genotype of either plant.
Every offspring would receive T from this plant and be tall, whatever the unknown's genotype.

options.content: A tall plant with white flowers (homozygous recessive for flower colour)
options.rationale: It is homozygous recessive for flower colour, not for height: being tall, it carries at least one T. The test-cross parent must be homozygous recessive for the gene being tested (tt).
This is a test cross: any dwarf offspring show the tall plant carries t.

explanation: In a test cross the unknown is crossed with a homozygous recessive plant (tt). If any offspring are dwarf, the tall plant must be Tt; if all of a large number are tall, it is almost certainly TT.
hints: Which parent would reveal exactly which allele the unknown passes on?

stem:
In peas, round seeds (**R**) are dominant to wrinkled seeds (**r**). Two plants grown from round seeds, plant 1 and plant 2, were each crossed with a plant grown from a wrinkled seed. The table shows the seeds produced.

| Cross | Round seeds | Wrinkled seeds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Plant 1 × wrinkled | 96 | 0 |
| Plant 2 × wrinkled | 53 | 49 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: What is the genotype of the wrinkled-seed parent?

options.rationale: A wrinkled seed shows the recessive phenotype, so it must be rr.
A heterozygote has round seeds.
RR seeds are round.

options.content: It cannot be known from its phenotype
options.rationale: The recessive phenotype always reveals the genotype.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: What is the most likely genotype of plant 1?

options.rationale: Rr × rr would be expected to give about half wrinkled seeds.
96 seeds and none wrinkled: every gamete carried R.
Plant 1 grew from a round seed, so it has at least one R.

options.content: It could be either RR or Rr with equal likelihood
options.rationale: With 96 seeds, an Rr plant would almost certainly have given some wrinkled seeds.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: What is the genotype of plant 2?

options.rationale: An RR plant cannot pass on r, so it could not produce wrinkled seeds with an rr plant.
Plant 2 grew from a round seed.
About half the seeds are wrinkled (53 : 49 is close to 1 : 1).

options.content: **RR** or **Rr**: the results cannot tell them apart
options.rationale: Even one wrinkled seed proves that plant 2 carries r.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain why a plant grown from a **wrinkled** seed is used in a test cross.

points.description: It is homozygous recessive (rr), so all its gametes carry r
So the phenotype of each offspring shows which allele (R or r) came from the unknown parent

parts.explanation: The wrinkled-seed plant is homozygous recessive (rr), so all of its gametes carry r. Each offspring's phenotype therefore depends only on the allele from the unknown plant: a round seed means it passed on R, and a wrinkled seed means it passed on r.

explanation: The wrinkled parent is rr. Plant 1 gave 96 round and no wrinkled seeds, so it is almost certainly RR. Plant 2 gave a ratio close to 1 : 1, so it must be Rr. A homozygous recessive parent reveals the allele carried by each gamete of the unknown.
workedSolution:
1. (a) Wrinkled is recessive, so the wrinkled parent is rr.
2. (b) RR × rr gives all Rr (round); 96 : 0 fits this.
3. (c) Rr × rr gives 1 Rr : 1 rr; $53 : 49 \approx 1.08 : 1$, close to 1 : 1.
4. (d) rr gametes all carry r, so each offspring shows the allele from the unknown parent.
hints: What ratio does Rr × rr give?

stem: Two heterozygous parents are expected to have children in the ratio 3 without a recessive feature : 1 with it. Why do real families often not show this exact ratio?

options.content: Because the dominant allele is lost in some gametes
options.rationale: Alleles are not lost; each gamete carries one or the other.

options.content: Because the ratio applies only to plants, not to people
options.rationale: The same rules of inheritance apply to plants, animals and people.

options.content: Because fertilisation is random, so the ratio is only a probability
options.rationale: Each fertilisation is an independent event; exact ratios are approached only with large numbers of offspring.

options.content: Because the recessive allele only ever shows in the first child of a family
options.rationale: Every child has the same chance, whatever their birth order.

explanation: Which sperm fertilises which egg is a matter of chance, so each child has a 1 in 4 chance of showing the recessive feature. In a small family the actual numbers often differ from 3 : 1; only large numbers come close to it.
hints: Is each child's genotype decided by chance?

stem: Students crossed two heterozygous pea plants with purple flowers. The offspring were 612 plants with purple flowers and 198 plants with white flowers. Calculate the ratio of purple to white flowers in the form $x : 1$. Give $x$ to two decimal places.
explanation: Divide both numbers by the white count: $612 \div 198 = 3.09$, so the ratio is $3.09 : 1$, close to the expected 3 : 1 for a cross between two heterozygotes.
workedSolution:
1. Ratio $= 612 : 198$.
2. Divide both by 198: $612 \div 198 = 3.0909\ldots$
3. To two decimal places, $x = 3.09$, so the ratio is $3.09 : 1$.
4. This is close to the expected 3 : 1.
hints: Divide the larger number by the smaller number.

stem: A farmer has a herd of horned cows and buys a polled bull. In cattle, polled (**P**) is dominant to horned (**p**). Explain how the farmer can use the bull's calves to find out whether the bull is homozygous or heterozygous. Use genetic diagrams in your answer. [6]

points.description: The horned cows are homozygous recessive (pp), so all their gametes carry p (this is a test cross)
Diagram 1: PP bull × pp cows; bull's gametes all P
All calves Pp, so all polled
Diagram 2: Pp bull × pp cows; bull's gametes P and p
Calves Pp and pp in a 1 : 1 ratio: about half polled, half horned
If any horned calf is born the bull is Pp; if a large number of calves are all polled the bull is (almost certainly) PP

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
The cows are horned, so they are homozygous recessive (pp) and every egg carries p. This is a test cross.

If the bull is PP: bull PP × cow pp; bull's gametes all P, cows' gametes all p; every calf is Pp, so all the calves are polled.

If the bull is Pp: bull Pp × cow pp; bull's gametes P or p, cows' gametes p; calves Pp and pp in a 1 : 1 ratio, so about half are polled and half horned.

The farmer records the calves. If even one horned calf is born, the bull must be Pp. If many calves are born and all are polled, the bull is almost certainly PP; the more calves, the more certain the conclusion.

explanation: A test cross with homozygous recessive cows shows which alleles the bull's sperm carry: any horned calf proves the bull is heterozygous.
hints: What genotype must a horned cow have?
Draw one diagram for each possible genotype of the bull.

stem: In pea plants, tall (**T**) is dominant to dwarf (**t**). Select **all** the crosses that could produce some **dwarf** offspring.

options.content: A heterozygous plant and a dwarf plant (**Tt** × **tt**)
options.rationale: Half of the offspring are expected to be tt.

options.content: A homozygous tall plant and a dwarf plant (**TT** × **tt**)
options.rationale: Every offspring gets T from the TT parent: all Tt, tall.
All offspring are tt, so all are dwarf.
All offspring are TT and tall.

options.content: A homozygous tall plant and a heterozygous plant (**TT** × **Tt**)
options.rationale: Every offspring gets T from the TT parent, so none can be tt.
Both parents can pass on t: 1 in 4 offspring tt.

explanation: A dwarf plant is tt, so it needs a t allele from each parent. That is possible only when neither parent is TT: Tt × Tt, Tt × tt and tt × tt.
hints: A dwarf offspring needs one t from each parent.

stem: Two parents are both carriers of the allele for albinism (**Aa**). They already have three children without albinism. True or false: their fourth child is certain to have albinism.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Not quite. Each child has a 1 in 4 chance of having albinism, whatever happened before. The fourth child is no more likely to have it than the first.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: Correct. Each fertilisation is independent, so every child has a 1 in 4 chance of having albinism.

explanation: A 1 in 4 probability applies to each child separately. Earlier children do not change the chance for the next one, so the fourth child has a 1 in 4 (25%) chance of having albinism.
hints: Do earlier births affect which sperm fertilises the next egg?

stem: An organism shows a **recessive** phenotype. What must its genotype be?

options.rationale: A heterozygote shows the dominant phenotype.
A recessive allele shows only when no dominant allele is present.
A homozygous dominant organism shows the dominant phenotype.
Those two genotypes both give the dominant phenotype.

explanation: A recessive allele is expressed only when there is no dominant allele present, so an organism with a recessive phenotype must be homozygous recessive.
hints: When is a recessive allele expressed?

stem: In cattle, polled (**P**) is dominant to horned (**p**). A pure-breeding polled bull is mated with pure-breeding horned cows. The F1 calves are later mated with each other to produce an F2 generation.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Give the genotype of the F1 calves.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: What is the phenotype of the F1 calves?

options.rationale: Every F1 calf is Pp, and P is dominant.
The horned allele is recessive, so it is hidden in Pp calves.
Pure-breeding parents give genetically identical F1 offspring.
With complete dominance, Pp calves are fully polled.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: What is the expected ratio of phenotypes in the F2?

options.rationale: That ratio comes from Pp × pp.
Both F1 parents carry p, so some F2 calves can be pp.
This mixes up genotypes and phenotypes: PP and Pp calves are both polled.
Pp × Pp gives 1 PP : 2 Pp : 1 pp.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: 36 F2 calves are born. How many would you expect to be horned?

explanation: PP × pp gives F1 calves that are all Pp and polled. Pp × Pp gives an F2 of 1 PP : 2 Pp : 1 pp, which is 3 polled : 1 horned; one quarter of 36 calves, 9, are expected to be horned.
workedSolution:
1. (a) Pure-breeding parents are PP and pp; their gametes are P and p, so every F1 calf is Pp.
2. (b) P is dominant, so all F1 calves are polled.
3. (c) Pp × Pp gives PP, Pp, Pp, pp: 3 polled : 1 horned.
4. (d) Horned $= \frac{1}{4} \times 36 = 9$ calves.
hints: Pure-breeding means homozygous.
